slides.say: Nadav and Amit have ninety cards together. Nadav has more cards than Amit. The difference between their numbers of cards is one fifth of the number of cards Nadav has. How many cards does Nadav have?

We could build an equation. Nadav has n cards, Amit has ninety minus n, and then we write the difference as one fifth of n. But why? We have the answers. The choices are numbers, and the story gives us conditions we can check.
Before we plug anything in, let's cross out what makes no sense. Nadav has more cards than Amit. So Nadav has more than half of the ninety cards, which means more than forty-five.
at: So Nadav has more than half

slides.say: So forty and forty-three are out, because they're less than half. For example, if Nadav had forty, Amit would have fifty, and then Amit would have more. So choice numbers one and two are out.
at: So forty and forty-three are out

slides.say: Two choices are left, forty-eight and fifty. Which one do we plug in? The more convenient one, the round one, fifty. It's easier to work with, and the right answer is often the round one.
Nadav has fifty cards. Together they have ninety, so Amit has ninety minus fifty, forty. And Nadav has more than Amit, fifty against forty, so that given is fine.

Now the last given, the difference has to be one fifth of Nadav's cards. The difference between them is fifty minus forty, ten. And one fifth of fifty is ten, because fifty divided by five is ten. Ten and ten, so fifty fits every given. Choice number four is our answer.
at: Choice number four is our answer

slides: This idea of starting with the convenient choices is very important. It saves work, and the exam often puts the right answer exactly there, among the round answers we'd want to try first. The exam is built to reward thinking, not long calculations. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
